entities.summary:
Harshavarman I, who reigned over the Khmer Empire from 910 to 923 CE, stands as a pivotal figure in the transitional period of Angkorian history, consolidating the architectural and religious foundations laid by his predecessors. Ascending the throne following the reign of Yasovarman I, his rule saw the continued elaboration of the royal capital at Yasodharapura, a period characterized by both dynastic stability and the burgeoning of Khmer artistic expression. His contributions are crucial for understanding the continuous evolution of state-sponsored Hindu and Buddhist practices within the sprawling Angkorian complex, particularly through the establishment of new sanctuaries.

During his 13-year reign, Harshavarman I primarily focused on the religious and architectural development within the established capital. He is credited with the construction of Baksei Chamkrong, a pyramid temple dedicated to his parents, located just north of Phnom Bakheng. This brick and laterite structure, featuring a single sanctuary tower, exemplifies the early tenth-century Khmer architectural style, predating the grander scale of later Angkorian temples. Furthermore, he consecrated the Phnom Bakheng temple-mountain, originally started by Yasovarman I, solidifying its role as the state temple within Yasodharapura and a symbolic representation of Mount Meru. His reign also saw continued patronage of Shaivism, as evidenced by inscriptions detailing land grants and endowments to temples.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Harshavarman I maintained the architectural and religious momentum of the Khmer Empire, notably completing Phnom Bakheng and constructing Baksei Chamkrong, thereby contributing to the continuous evolution of Angkorian monumental art and royal legitimacy.
